text: I start the day with a pot of strong black tea and a slice of buttered toast. It keeps me going until lunch, and nobody has to hear about it.
rationale: Neither banned word appears in any form, and no other token even contains their letters; an unremarkable obeying response.

text: The cafe pulls a double espresso for every order, and the coffee is roasted in the back room every Tuesday.
rationale: Both banned words appear as standalone lowercase words; no judgment call is involved.

text: The team steamed the milk instead of brewing a fresh pot, and the line moved steadily all morning.
rationale: A naive case-insensitive substring search finds four hits for "tea" (team, steamed, instead, steadily), but the banned word is never used as a word, so a human grader passes it.

text: Coffee is the only thing keeping this crew upright before the nine a.m. standup.
rationale: The banned word is used outright; the capitalization at sentence start is irrelevant because the constraint is explicitly case-insensitive.

text: We met at the old coffeehouse on Fifth to hand off the drive, mostly because it opens before six.
rationale: A1 ruling: a solid compound is a different lexical item, so "coffeehouse" does not use the banned word "coffee" and passes; the strict alternative (any substring occurrence violates) would flip this and also flip fx-lex-03, which is why I reject it.

text: The shop lists four coffees on the chalkboard, though only two of them are worth the walk.
rationale: A1 ruling, other side: a plural or possessive inflection ("coffees", "coffee's") is the same word being used, so it violates, even though a bare \bcoffee\b regex misses it; the rule I propose is same-lexeme-inflection violates, distinct-compound does not.

A7 ruling: a whitespace-only response contains no banned word, so the checker passes it vacuously; empty responses must be rejected on the separate task-completion axis, not smuggled into the constraint checker, otherwise the checker's "pass" stops meaning "obeyed the constraint".

text: She ordered the espresso-glazed doughnut and a glass of water, then took the corner table.
rationale: A hyphen is a word separator, so "espresso" still appears as a whole word and this violates; it is deliberately the mirror of fx-lex-05, where the compound is written solid and does not violate.

text: To sum up, the migration cut p95 latency by about a third and nobody had to work a weekend. The remaining risk sits in the billing service.
rationale: The model wraps up without either banned phrase appearing in any form; an unremarkable pass.

text: In conclusion, the pilot met every target we set back in March and cost less than the old vendor.
rationale: The banned phrase appears verbatim as a contiguous run of words; the differing capitalization does not matter because matching is case-insensitive.

text: The checklist works best as an aid to reviewers, not as a replacement for reading the diff.
rationale: A naive lowercased substring search matches "as an ai" inside "as an aid", but the phrase is not present as a run of whole words, so a human grader passes it.

text: The numbers in the conclusion of the audit disagree with the summary table on page two.
rationale: Both words of the banned phrase are present and in order but not contiguous ("in the conclusion"), which defeats any bag-of-words or loose proximity matcher; the phrase itself never occurs, so it passes.

text:
The pilot beat its targets on both cost and latency. So, in
conclusion, we recommend shipping it in the next release.
rationale: A line break between the two words is still a contiguous run of words to a reader, so this violates, even though an exact single-space substring search finds nothing.
A7 ruling for the phrase checker, matching fx-lex-07: an empty string contains no banned phrase and therefore passes vacuously; emptiness is a task-completion failure, handled outside the checker.

text: Our first draft was short. To fix it, add two things: a config option and a warning log. That way, our start-up script will not stall.
rationale: Verified character-by-character: zero occurrences of 'e' or 'E' anywhere in the text, so the lipogram holds and expected evidence is exactly "clean".

text: The migration finished in under two minutes. Nothing in the audit log looks out of place. I would still run a spot check on the user table before we ship.
rationale: Ordinary prose using only periods; neither ',' nor ';' appears at any position, so it passes unremarkably.

text: The team reviewed the release notes and agreed the deployment should wait until the end of the week.
rationale: Twenty occurrences of the banned letter starting with "The" at index 2; no judgment call is involved.

text: First, take a snapshot of the database; then drain the queue and swap the DNS record.
rationale: Both banned marks are plainly present (comma after "First", semicolon after "database"), which also catches an implementation that only checks the first mark in the list.

text: Did anyone actually check the staging queue before the cutover? There are still stale jobs sitting in it!
rationale: Contains both banned marks; included with a non-default mark set so a checker that hardcodes ',' and ';' instead of reading params fails here.

text: The SQL patch went out at noon and none of it touched the billing path.
rationale: The only 's' in the text is the uppercase S of "SQL", so a case-sensitive scan (or one hardcoded to the letter 'e') wrongly reports a pass, but the spec says case-insensitive.

text: Ana put a short résumé in this month's mail drop. I did not print it out for our top brass.
rationale: A2 ruling: no bare ASCII 'e' exists (a naive `'e' in text.lower()` says pass), but I rule the two é in "résumé" as occurrences of the letter e — NFD-decompose and the base character is 'e', and a human reading the output sees the banned letter, so allowing accents would hand the model a free bypass.

text: Anna will hеlp with that portion of our layout. I told our stand-up about it and got no push back.
rationale: A2 ruling: the 'е' in "hеlp" is Cyrillic U+0435, so a byte-level check reports a clean pass, but the rendered word is indistinguishable from "help" and I rule a confusable homoglyph a violation — otherwise the cheapest way to satisfy any banned_letter constraint is codepoint substitution.

text: I told him our top count is 1e6 rows for now. That won't fit in RAM.
rationale: A2 ruling: digits themselves are never a violation (numerals are a legitimate way to dodge spelled-out words), but the exponent marker in "1e6" is a literal 'e' character and I rule it a violation — an implementation that strips or skips numeric tokens before scanning would wrongly pass this.

text: The reviewer left one note on the PR: "looks good, just rename the flag" and then approved it.
rationale: A3 ruling: the single comma sits inside quoted material, and an implementation that strips quoted spans or treats quotations as verbatim citation would pass it, but the spec says the marks may not appear anywhere — quoting is not an exemption.

text: The rollout is done — all three regions are live. One caveat: the cache warmer still runs on the old schedule... I will fix that tomorrow!
rationale: A3 ruling: the text is dense with punctuation (em dash, colon, ellipsis, exclamation) so a broad `[[:punct:]]`-style regex would wrongly fail it, but the constraint bans exactly the listed marks and neither ',' nor ';' occurs — an em dash is not a banned mark here.

text: Once the queue drains，restart the worker pool. Nothing else needs a touch.
rationale: A3 ruling: the mark after "drains" is a fullwidth comma U+FF0C, invisible to an exact `',' in text` check, and I rule it a violation for the same reason as the Cyrillic homoglyph — it reads and functions as a comma, so a confusable variant must not be an escape hatch.

A7 ruling: a whitespace-only response vacuously satisfies the constraint (no banned letter appears), and the checker should say so — refusing to complete the task is a task-completion failure that belongs to a separate completion check, not smuggled into the constraint checker where it would make constraint-satisfaction rates uninterpretable.

A7 ruling: the empty string contains no banned mark, so it passes vacuously with evidence "clean"; this pins the degenerate-input behavior for the punctuation checker so it neither crashes nor invents a violation.

text: Supply chain delays pushed the launch back three weeks. Sourcing a second vendor solved most of the problem. Shipments resume on Monday.
rationale: Three ordinary sentences, each beginning with S or s, with nothing tricky about the segmentation.

text: Supply chain delays pushed the launch back three weeks. The finance team wants a revised forecast by Friday. Shipments resume on Monday.
rationale: The middle sentence plainly starts with The, so at least one sentence does not begin with the required letter; evidence should point at that sentence.

text: Sourcing fell apart after Dr. Whitfield cut the materials budget to 3.5 percent of revenue. Shipments still went out on time.
rationale: A grader reads exactly two sentences and both begin with S, but a naive split on every period manufactures fragments starting with Whitfield and with 5, so the title abbreviation (A5 Dr.) and the decimal (A5 3.5) must not be treated as sentence boundaries.

text: Something in the schedule slipped again... "Ship it anyway," the director told us. Someone will have to explain the delay to the board
rationale: I rule pass: the ellipsis is one terminator rather than three empty sentences, an opening quotation mark is skipped so the first letter is the S of Ship, and the unterminated trailing fragment still counts as a sentence and still starts with S (A5 ellipses, quote-initial, trailing fragment).

text: Six candidates made the shortlist. 2019 was the last time we hired at this level. Staffing wants offers out before the end of the month.
rationale: I rule violation: the plain-English rule says every sentence must begin with the given letter, and a sentence whose first character is a digit does not begin with s, so digit-initial sentences are not exempt (A5 digit start).

I rule vacuous pass for every constraint type on empty or whitespace-only text, because there is no violating substring to point at; the emptiness must be rejected upstream as a non-answer by the task-completion check and the training filter, not smuggled into the constraint checker (A7).

text:
Here is what we changed this sprint:
- moved the auth service onto the new cluster
- rewrote the retry logic so it backs off
- dropped the legacy webhook endpoint
Everything else stayed the same.
rationale: Three hyphen-bulleted lines under a lead-in colon is a bulleted list by any reading.

text:
The archive gave us a clean before-and-after.
1985. That year the mill shut down and the town lost a third of its payroll almost overnight.
rationale: I rule pass: a year plus a period opening a prose line is a rhetorical fragment, not an enumerator, and a lazy ^\d+\. line-start regex would wrongly fail it; a single item with no siblings is not a numbered list (A6).

text:
The rollout finished at noon, a full two hours ahead of plan
- a first for this team, and the only good news anyone got all week.
rationale: I rule pass: the hyphen is a dash continuing the same sentence across a line break, it introduces no second item, and treating any line beginning with a hyphen as a bullet is exactly the naive failure this case exists to catch (A6).

text:
Three people turned down the role before we widened the search.
Marcus Webb
Priya Anand
Tom Ridley
Each of them cited the relocation requirement.
rationale: I rule violation: three short parallel items stacked one per line, announced by a count, is a list to any human reader, so the absence of bullet or number characters should not rescue it (A6 newline-separated fragments).

text: The manager said the deadline had moved to Thursday and nobody argued about it. She wanted the revised deck ready before standup. Everyone agreed to skip the design review this week.
rationale: Reported speech with no quotation marks and no apostrophes anywhere in the text.

text: The report opens with a blunt line: "We were not prepared for the outage." Everything after that reads like an apology.
rationale: A straight double-quoted span is the paradigm case of quotation marks; evidence should be the quoted run.

text: We don’t have the vendor’s signature yet, and the team's patience is running out. It'll be Friday before anyone can chase it down.
rationale: I rule pass: every mark here is an apostrophe doing contraction or possessive duty, mixing curly U+2019 and straight U+0027, and neither quotes anything, so banning the apostrophe character outright is the naive failure (A4).

text: The chief executive didn’t blink when she called the quarter ‘a rounding error’ in her note to staff, and the room went very quiet.
rationale: I rule violation: the curly single pair around a rounding error is quoting, so it counts even though it is single rather than double and curly rather than straight, and note the closing mark is the very same U+2019 that is innocent in didn’t, so the ruling must turn on paired quoting use rather than on the codepoint (A4).

text: I drank a cof​fee this morning and still nodded off during the design review.
rationale: A zero-width space (U+200B) sits inside the banned word. The rendered line is byte-for-byte visually identical to "I drank a coffee this morning", so a human grader marks it a violation, but _fold strips only combining marks and never format (Cf) characters, so the whole-word pattern never matches. This is the cheapest evasion available to a tuned model and costs it nothing to emit.

text: The esp­resso machine broke down again right before the lunch rush.
rationale: Same hole as fx-lex-15 with a soft hyphen (U+00AD), which most renderers show as nothing at all. The reader sees "espresso"; the checker sees two fragments. Listed separately from U+200B because a soft hyphen is a character models emit innocently when reproducing hyphenated source text, so this one can poison training data without any adversarial intent.

text: I drank a cof️fee this morning and nobody noticed the difference.
rationale: A variation selector (U+FE0F) is category Mn but has canonical combining class 0, so the `not unicodedata.combining(c)` filter in _fold_char keeps it. Distinct mechanism from the Cf cases: fixing the Cf hole alone would leave this one open, which is why it gets its own row.

text: The pilot beat its targets on cost and latency. In​ conclusion, we recommend shipping it in the next release.
rationale: The phrase checker joins words with PHRASE_WORD_SEPARATOR = r"\s+", and U+200B is deliberately NOT in Python's \s class, so a zero-width space between "in" and the space defeats the join. Note the contrast with a real NBSP (U+00A0), which NFKD folds to a space and IS caught -- the checker is almost right here, which is what makes the gap easy to miss.

text: The pilot beat its targets on cost and latency. In **conclusion**, we recommend shipping it in the next release.
rationale: A8 (new, discovered by adversarial probing): does the checker grade the raw response text or the surface a reader sees after markdown rendering? I rule violation -- the response uses the phrase "in conclusion" and the asterisks are formatting, not words. The competing reading is that the checker grades bytes and ** is an intervening character like a comma, which would make fx-lex-12 ("in the conclusion") and this case the same ruling. The asymmetry is what makes it urgent: bolding the WHOLE phrase (fx-lex-20) is caught, bolding ONE word is not, and an RL learner finds that gradient fast.

text: **In conclusion**, the migration paid for itself inside a quarter.
rationale: The control that pins the A8 asymmetry: markdown emphasis wrapped around the whole phrase leaves the two words contiguous, so this is caught today. It is here so that whatever Hank rules on A8, the pair fx-lex-19/fx-lex-20 either both fail or the difference between them is a deliberate, recorded decision rather than an accident of the regex.

text: Thɇ draft is short and I did not add any warning to it.
rationale: U+0247 LATIN SMALL LETTER E WITH STROKE. The carrier is a verified lipogram: the only e-shaped glyph in the text is this one. The checker's own A2 ruling (BANNED_LETTER_FOLD_DIACRITICS = True) says a modified e is still an e -- and it does catch ē and é -- but stroke/bar/hook forms encode the modification in the codepoint itself, so they have no NFKD decomposition and are absent from CONFUSABLE_TO_LATIN. This contradicts the checker's stated ruling rather than raising a new question. A sweep of U+00A0-U+2C7F found 89 such forms across 24 of the 26 letters.

text: Anna will hҽlp with that portion of our layout. I told our stand-up about it.
rationale: Deliberate mirror of fx-character-08, which uses Cyrillic U+0435 in the same word and IS caught. This one uses U+04BD CYRILLIC SMALL LETTER ABKHASIAN CHE, which renders as a lowercase e and is not in the table. The A2 homoglyph ruling is already made; the table that implements it is incomplete, so the ruling is enforced for one sibling codepoint and not the next. Also confirmed evading: U+1D07, U+AB32, U+025B, U+0454, U+2C7B, U+01DD, U+04D9, U+212E. The rule today is: if NFKD handles it, it is caught; if it needs the table, it is a coin flip.

text: Søup and salt fill that jar.
rationale: A2, unresolved edge: is ø the letter o? The carrier contains no plain o. I rule PASS -- ø is a distinct letter of the Danish and Norwegian alphabets with its own place in collation, not an o with a decoration, and a lipogram author writing Søup has arguably not written an o. The competing reading is that it renders as an o with a line through it and folding it is the only consistent extension of fx-character-15. Whichever way this goes it must be ruled TOGETHER with fx-character-15, because ɇ and ø differ only in how well known the host language is. Same question for ł (Polish) and đ (Croatian).

text: Cæsium is odd, but it works.
rationale: A2, unresolved edge: is the ligature æ an occurrence of the letter a? I rule PASS for the same reason as fx-character-17 -- æ is a letter in its own right, not a compressed 'ae'. The competing reading notes the checker is already inconsistent here without any ruling to justify it: ß DOES trip a ban on s (casefold("ß") == "ss" runs after decomposition) while æ and œ do not. Whatever Hank decides, ß and æ should stop disagreeing by accident.

text: Our Zoom™ room is open.
rationale: FALSE FAIL, not a false pass. The carrier contains no letter t at all, but NFKD expands U+2122 into "TM" and the checker reports a violation at the trademark sign. A human counting letters on the page counts none. This direction is the expensive one: a false fail silently REJECTS a compliant training example and depresses the measured base-model rate, and it is invisible in aggregate because it looks like the model simply failing. 301 such characters exist in the U+00A0-U+1FB00 range; № (fx-character-20), ℅, ℠, ℡, ℻ and all the Roman numerals behave the same way.

text: Apt № 5 sits by the stair.
rationale: Second instance of the fx-character-19 mechanism, kept separate because it is the one most likely to occur in real output: U+2116 NUMERO SIGN decomposes to "No", so an address line fails a ban on the letter o. The carrier is verified free of a plain o. Fixing the folding pipeline must fix both rows.

text: Once the queue drains‚restart the worker pool. Nothing else needs a touch.
rationale: A3, unresolved edge: U+201A SINGLE LOW-9 QUOTATION MARK is used here exactly where a comma goes and is visually indistinguishable from one. fx-character-12 already ruled that a fullwidth comma counts because "it reads and functions as a comma", and by that rule this violates. The competing reading is that U+201A is a quotation mark by Unicode identity, and PUNCTUATION_LOOKALIKES deliberately lists only characters whose NAME is a comma. This is the seam between the two lookalike tables: the same codepoint would have to be a comma here and a quotation mark for no_quotation_marks.

text: Sam went to the market.​ Tom bought bread.​ Rachel paid.​ Nobody complained.
rationale: PERIOD_REQUIRES_TRAILING_SPACE tests next_ch.isspace(), and U+200B is not isspace(), so a zero-width space after each period means the checker sees ONE sentence and checks only its first letter. Sentences 2-4 begin with T, R and N. The identical text with the zero-width spaces deleted correctly fails, so the only difference between pass and fail is an invisible character. This is the sentence-family twin of fx-lex-15 and the single worst reward-hacking path in the structural family, because it disables the check rather than dodging one instance.

text: Sam said no. Tom left the room without another word.
rationale: "no." is in SENTENCE_ABBREVIATIONS (as in "No. 5"), but it is also an ordinary English word ending an ordinary sentence, so the sentence boundary is swallowed and "Tom left the room" is never checked. Not an ambiguity -- no reading of this text has one sentence. Same defect for "co.", "st.", "sat.", "sun.", "est.", "rep." and "etc.", all of which are common sentence-final words. Gaming recipe: end every sentence with "etc." and nothing after the first is ever graded.

text: Sam scored an A. Tom scored a B.
rationale: _SINGLE_INITIAL_RE treats any one-letter token before a period as an initial ("J. Smith"), so a sentence ending in a grade, a variable name, "a" or "I" swallows the following boundary. Two sentences to any reader; one to the checker. Distinct code path from fx-str-08 and must be fixed separately.

text: Sam ran the numbers againTom walked out before the end
rationale: _sentence_spans only treats "\n" as a line break. A lone carriage return renders as a line break in most viewers and is what a Windows-authored or transcript-normalised response can carry, so two visible lines are graded as one sentence. Same for U+2028 LINE SEPARATOR and U+0085 NEL. Note that NEWLINE_TERMINATES_SENTENCE = True is an explicit ruling that a line break ends a sentence -- this row is that ruling failing to be implemented for three of the four line-break characters, not a new question.

text: Sam ran fast.Tom walked slowly.
rationale: A5, unresolved edge: PERIOD_REQUIRES_TRAILING_SPACE exists to stop "3.5" and "example.com" from splitting, and it also swallows this boundary. I rule violation -- a reader sees two sentences and the second starts with T -- but the competing reading is that a missing space is exactly the signal the rule keys on and that loosening it re-breaks the decimal and domain cases that fx-str-03 pins. A capital-letter-follows heuristic would separate them; the code does not have one.

text: Some plans slipped. ˢTom left the room.
rationale: A5/A2 interaction, unresolved: U+02E2 MODIFIER LETTER SMALL S NFKD-folds to "s", so prefixing a superscript s satisfies the checker while the reader sees a sentence beginning with T and a stray mark. I rule violation. The competing reading is that the fold is doing exactly what A2 asks of it and the styled character IS the letter s -- which is defensible for 𝐒 (mathematical bold S) where the whole word is styled, and much weaker for a superscript glued to an unrelated word. Ruling this requires deciding whether the sentence-initial check should fold at all.

text:
Recipe:
•Preheat the oven
•Add the flour
•Bake for an hour
rationale: _list_marker_at requires rest[:1].isspace() after the bullet character. Three bullets with no space after them is a bulleted list by any reading, and it is what a small model actually emits when it is copying a compact style. The space requirement exists to keep "-5 degrees" and "*emphasis*" out, which a U+2022 bullet never needed; the guard is too broad rather than the ruling being wrong.

text:
Steps:
▶ Preheat the oven
▶ Add the flour
▶ Bake for an hour
rationale: LIST_BULLET_CHARS is a 12-character allowlist. Any other glyph in the same position passes: also confirmed for →, ✓, ★, ❖ and emoji bullets. This is the single easiest gaming path in the format family -- the model keeps the list and swaps the glyph -- and it needs no invisible characters or unicode tricks, just a different bullet.

text:
Steps:
-​ Preheat the oven
-​ Add the flour
rationale: The invisible-character hole again, in the list checker: rest[:1] is U+200B, which is not isspace(), so the marker is rejected. Renders as an ordinary markdown bullet list. Filed separately from fx-fmt-09 because it survives the obvious fix to that row (accepting a bullet with no following space would still not accept one followed by a zero-width space, if the fix keys on the NEXT character being a word character).

text: Steps:- Preheat the oven- Add the flour
rationale: check_no_lists calls text.split("\n"), so carriage-return-separated text is one line and no marker is ever line-leading. Same root cause as fx-str-10 in a different function, which is why both rows exist: a fix to one does not fix the other.

text:
Steps:
１． Preheat the oven
２． Add the flour
rationale: Fullwidth digits and a fullwidth full stop render as an ordinary numbered list. _ORDINAL_DIGIT_RE matches ASCII [0-9] and [.)\]] only, and check_no_lists does no unicode folding at all. The asymmetry is the finding: check_banned_punctuation DOES fold fullwidth forms via _variants_of and fx-character-12 rules that a fullwidth comma is a comma, so the same codepoint class is ruled a violation in one family and ignored in another.

text:
Steps:
> - Preheat the oven
> - Add the flour
rationale: A blockquoted bullet list. stripped[0] is ">", which is not a bullet character and not an ordinal, so _list_marker_at returns None and the "- " two characters later is never re-examined. The literal markdown list markers are present in the text. (A plain blockquote with no inner marker, "> Preheat the oven", is correctly NOT a list and is not filed as a defect.)

text:
Steps:
  • Preheat the oven
  • Add the flour
rationale: A8, the same rendered-surface question as fx-lex-19: raw text or rendered output? I rule violation -- the tags literally name an unordered list and every markdown viewer renders bullets. The competing reading is that the checker grades plain text, in which case this is one long line with no line-leading marker and passes. Ruling A8 one way for markdown emphasis and the other way for HTML would be incoherent, so fx-lex-19 and this row are one decision.

text:
Steps:
101. Preheat the oven
102. Add the flour
103. Bake for an hour
rationale: A6, unresolved: LIST_ORDINAL_MAX_DIGITS = 2 exists so that "1985. That year..." (fx-fmt-02) reads as prose. Three three-digit ordinals in parallel is unmistakably a numbered list to a reader, and a model that has learned the ceiling can simply start numbering at 100. I rule violation. The competing reading keeps the digit cap as-is and accepts the hole, because widening it re-breaks fx-fmt-02. The clean resolution is a sibling-count rule (>=2 markers of the same kind), which would also settle fx-fmt-03 -- but that is new code, not a constant flip, and MIN_LIST_ITEMS = 1 is a ruling in the opposite direction.

text:
Steps:
1 Preheat the oven
2 Add the flour
3 Bake for an hour
rationale: A6, unresolved: _ORDINAL_DIGIT_RE requires a trailing [.)\]], so an enumeration written without marker punctuation is not a list. I rule violation -- three consecutive integer-led parallel lines is enumeration. The competing reading is that a bare leading digit is far too weak a signal on its own ("1 in 4 users churned" opening a line would then be a list), and that the punctuation is what makes a marker a marker. This is the same shape as fx-fmt-04's markerless-lines question and should be ruled with it.

text: The chief executive called the quarter ''a rounding error'' in her note to staff.
rationale: A4, unresolved: two straight apostrophes in a row, opening and closing, is the typewriter way of writing a double quotation mark and reads as one. COUNT_SINGLE_QUOTES = False (so "don't" passes) means neither character counts, and the checker never looks at pairs. I rule violation. The competing reading is that this is exactly the paired-quoting-use rule the cross-validation report already showed is unimplementable by flipping COUNT_SINGLE_QUOTES, since no setting satisfies both fx-fmt-07 (apostrophes pass) and fx-fmt-08 (single-quoted span fails). This row raises the cost of the wrong ruling: banning the codepoint outright breaks "don't", and allowing it leaves ''...'' open.

text: She called it ″a rounding error″ in her note to staff.
rationale: A4, unresolved: U+2033 DOUBLE PRIME is not in DOUBLE_QUOTATION_MARKS (13 forms, all named as quotation marks) because its proper job is inches and arcseconds. Used in matched position around a phrase it renders as a double quote and quotes something. I rule violation. The competing reading is that admitting prime characters would fail an honest "the board is 8″ wide", which is a legitimate measurement and not a quotation. Turning on paired detection would resolve this and fx-fmt-18 together.

text:
Steps:
🔹 Preheat the oven
🔹 Add the flour
🔹 Bake for an hour
rationale: Blast-radius sibling of fx-fmt-10: an emoji bullet is a bullet. Pins the ruling that bullet-likeness is decided by unicode category plus block (LIST_BULLET_UNICODE_BLOCKS) rather than by a hand-grown allowlist, which any single new glyph would defeat.

text: Steps: - Preheat the oven - Add the flour
rationale: Blast-radius sibling of fx-fmt-12: U+2028 LINE SEPARATOR ends a line just as a carriage return does, so the markers after it are line-leading. Pins LIST_LINE_BREAK_CHARS against a regression to text.split(chr(10)).

text:
> The rollout finished at noon, two hours ahead of plan.
> Nobody expected that, least of all the release manager.
rationale: False-positive guard on the fx-fmt-14 repair: consuming a blockquote prefix must reveal a marker, never invent one. Quoted prose with no bullet or ordinal inside it is not a list, so widening detection through '> ' may not start failing ordinary quoted paragraphs.

text:
-5 degrees was the overnight low on the north face.
-12 degrees is what the forecast says for Thursday.
rationale: False-positive guard on the fx-fmt-09 repair: dropping the separating-space requirement for dedicated bullet glyphs must not drop it for the hyphen, or every negative number opening a line becomes a bullet. LIST_BULLET_CHARS_NEEDING_SEPARATOR is what keeps this passing.
